[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental variation in high-skill immigration (e.g., H-1B visa lotteries) combined with regional firm dynamism measures (e.g., firm entry rates from the Business Dynamics Statistics). — This source would provide causal identification of the effect of high-skill immigration on low-skill wages, allowing comparison across regions with high vs. low firm dynamism, directly testing the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural labor market models incorporating firm heterogeneity and endogenous entry (e.g., search-and-matching models with firm dynamics). — Such models can simulate how the wage response to high-skill immigration varies with firm dynamism, clarifying the mechanisms (e.g., job creation, competition, or complementarity) and generating testable predictions.

[PATH:literature] Existing literature on local labor market impacts of immigration, focusing on heterogeneity by local economic dynamism (e.g., studies using U.S. metropolitan area panel data from 2000–2020). — A systematic review of empirical studies that estimate wage effects of high-skill immigration by regional firm entry rates can reveal whether the hypothesized differential effect is consistently observed or refuted.

qualifier.geographic: United States, metropolitan statistical areas with below-median firm entry rates

[PATH:empirical] Quarterly Workforce Indicators (QWI) from the U.S. Census Bureau combined with H-1B visa data — Linking regional firm dynamism measures (e.g., job creation rates, establishment entry/exit) to high-skill immigration flows and native low-skill wage/employment outcomes can directly test the conditional effect hypothesized.

[PATH:literature] Borjas, G.J. (2003). 'The Labor Demand Curve Is Downward Sloping: Reexamining the Impact of Immigration on the Labor Market.' Quarterly Journal of Economics — This foundational work provides the canonical framework for analyzing immigration's wage effects and can be extended to examine how low firm dynamism moderates those effects, offering theoretical grounding and testable predictions.

[PATH:empirical] Regional variation in firm dynamism indices (e.g., from the Kauffman Foundation or BDS) and matched CPS/ACS microdata — Using a difference-in-differences or instrumental variables approach across U.S. metro areas with varying levels of firm dynamism would isolate whether the positive effect of high-skill immigration on low-skill natives is stronger or weaker in low-dynamism regions.

C007.subject: immigration of high-skill workers
C007.predicate: reduces wage inequality between high-skill and low-skill workers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: immigration of high-skill workers regions with low firm dynamism]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental study comparing high-skill immigration shocks across U.S. commuting zones with high vs. low firm dynamism (e.g., using H-1B visa lottery or variation in university R&D spending). — A difference-in-differences or instrumental variable approach can isolate whether the complementary demand effect (increased innovation, firm creation, and demand for low-skill services) dominates the labor supply competition effect only in low-dynamism regions, where incumbent firms have market power and thus may pass on productivity gains to low-skill workers.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural labor market model with heterogeneous firms and skill-specific production functions, calibrated to regional data on firm entry rates, patenting, and wage distributions. — A model that explicitly nests both the labor supply competition channel and the complementary demand channel can simulate counterfactual scenarios. Testing the model's predictions for regions with low firm dynamism (e.g., low startup rates) can reveal parameter ranges under which high-skill immigration reduces wage inequality, providing a theoretical benchmark for empirical work.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on high-skill immigration and local wage inequality, stratified by measures of regional firm dynamism (e.g., business churn rate, concentration indices). — A systematic review and meta-regression can synthesize heterogeneous findings across different contexts and time periods. If the effect of high-skill immigration on reducing wage inequality is consistently larger or only present in low-dynamism regions, this would support the hypothesis; if no such pattern emerges, it would cast doubt on the proposed mechanism.

qualifier.mechanism: complementary demand effect outweighs labor supply competition

[PATH:empirical] Borjas (2003) 'The Labor Demand Curve Is Downward Sloping: Reexamining the Impact of Immigration on the Labor Market' and subsequent spatial correlation studies using variation across U.S. metropolitan areas — This classic work provides the baseline methodology for estimating wage effects of immigration on native workers. Extending it to focus on high-skill immigration in high-dynamism metros with land-use regulation would directly test whether regulatory constraints amplify negative wage spillovers on low-skill natives.

[PATH:theoretical] Hsieh & Moretti (2019) 'Housing Constraints and Spatial Misallocation' and related work on regulatory barriers to production adjustment — This research quantifies how land-use regulation and other barriers limit firm expansion and housing supply, which in turn constrains labor demand adjustments. Applying this framework to high-skill immigration shocks would clarify the mechanism through which regulatory frictions could depress low-skill wages, offering a theoretical foundation for the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Peri & Sparber (2009) 'Task Specialization, Immigration, and Wages' and recent panel data on U.S. commuting zones by skill level and firm dynamism — This work emphasizes task specialization and complementarity between high- and low-skill workers. By re-estimating the model on a sample restricted to high-dynamism, high-regulation metros post-2000, one could isolate whether the usual positive complementarity breaks down under regulatory constraints, thus refuting or confirming the wage-depression claim.

scope.domain: labor economics, regulatory frictions, regional dynamism
